title: Essential Tremor: Action Tremor, Function, and the Mimic Check
bottomLine: Essential tremor is usually a bilateral action/postural tremor syndrome diagnosed clinically after medication, metabolic and parkinsonian/cerebellar mimics are considered. Treat when disability or distress justifies therapy, not because a tremor is visible.
recognize: Hand/forearm action tremor is most common; head or voice tremor may occur.
Family history and alcohol responsiveness can be supportive but are not diagnostic requirements.
differentiate: Parkinson tremor is commonly rest-predominant with bradykinesia/rigidity; cerebellar tremor has intention/ataxic features; enhanced physiologic tremor can follow stimulants, anxiety, hyperthyroidism or medications.
assessment: Characterize rest/posture/action components, symmetry, handwriting/function, gait, bradykinesia/rigidity, cerebellar signs, medications/substances, thyroid symptoms and family history.
workup: Typical essential tremor with a normal neurologic examination usually needs no brain imaging; use targeted thyroid/metabolic or imaging studies only when the phenotype is atypical.
management: Use functional impact and patient preference to decide on therapy; propranolol or primidone are common first-line options when appropriate.
Refractory disabling tremor warrants movement-disorder referral for additional medication, botulinum or procedural options.
medicationSafety: Propranolol may be unsuitable with significant bradycardia, hypotension or reactive-airway disease; primidone can cause sedation/ataxia and requires cautious initiation.
redFlags: Tremor beginning with major systemic/toxic symptoms
counselling: Discuss caffeine/stimulant contributors and practical adaptive strategies without implying stress is the cause of the disorder.
followUp: Track function and adverse effects rather than tremor amplitude alone.
examTrap: Ordering MRI for a classic longstanding bilateral action tremor with a normal neurologic examination instead of first distinguishing essential tremor from parkinsonism and medication/metabolic causes.
oneLinePearl: Essential tremor is an action-tremor syndrome; treat disability, not visibility.
sourceBasis: Canadian Neurological Society/Choosing Wisely Canada diagnostic-stewardship principles

title: Myasthenia Gravis: Fatigable Weakness and the Respiratory Crisis You Cannot Miss
bottomLine: Myasthenia gravis causes fluctuating fatigable skeletal-muscle weakness, often ocular or bulbar, with preserved sensation. Confirm the diagnosis with antibody/electrodiagnostic pathways and treat respiratory or bulbar deterioration as possible myasthenic crisis requiring urgent ventilatory assessment.
recognize: Ptosis/diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, neck/proximal weakness and fatigability are typical.
Sensation is preserved and pupils are usually unaffected.
differentiate: Lambert-Eaton often has autonomic symptoms and facilitation with exercise; botulism can affect pupils/autonomic function; stroke produces focal fixed deficits rather than fatigable weakness.
assessment: Assess swallowing, speech, cough strength, respiratory effort, secretion handling, infection/medication triggers and pregnancy status in addition to limb/ocular weakness.
workup: Use acetylcholine-receptor and other appropriate antibodies plus electrodiagnostic testing; image the mediastinum for thymic disease after diagnosis according to specialty pathway.
During possible crisis, serial respiratory mechanics and blood gas/clinical ventilation assessment matter more than pulse oximetry alone.
management: Use pyridostigmine and immunotherapy under neurology guidance; thymectomy is indication-specific.
Possible crisis with bulbar/respiratory weakness requires hospital/ICU-level evaluation and IVIG/plasma-exchange pathways as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Several medications can worsen neuromuscular transmission; review new antibiotics, magnesium, sedatives and other implicated drugs rather than assuming disease progression.
Excess cholinesterase inhibitor can also worsen weakness and secretions; dosing changes require clinical review.
counselling: Teach early crisis warning signs and the importance of medication/intercurrent-illness review.
followUp: Coordinate neurology follow-up for symptom control, steroid-sparing strategy, thymic evaluation and pregnancy planning when relevant.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with worsening dysphagia and dyspnea because oxygen saturation is still normal.
oneLinePearl: In myasthenia, ventilation can fail before oxygen saturation looks dramatic.
sourceBasis: International consensus myasthenia guidance where a current Canadian national CPG is not available

title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Median-Nerve Pattern Before Testing
bottomLine: Carpal tunnel syndrome is a median-nerve compression syndrome diagnosed primarily from the characteristic sensory/motor pattern and examination. Reserve electrodiagnostic or imaging studies for diagnostic uncertainty, severe deficits or procedural planning rather than every classic mild case.
recognize: Numbness/paresthesia in thumb, index, middle and radial ring finger, nocturnal symptoms and hand shaking for relief are common.
Thenar weakness/atrophy indicates more advanced nerve injury.
differentiate: Cervical radiculopathy, proximal median neuropathy, polyneuropathy and arthritis can mimic hand symptoms.
The thenar eminence may be spared sensorially because its palmar cutaneous branch travels outside the tunnel.
assessment: Map sensory symptoms, thumb abduction/opposition, thenar bulk, neck/radicular signs, diabetes/thyroid/pregnancy risk and occupational repetition.
workup: Electrodiagnostic testing is useful for atypical symptoms, severe weakness, differential diagnosis or before surgery when required; routine wrist MRI is not needed for typical CTS.
management: Night neutral-position wrist splinting and activity modification are reasonable initial therapy for mild/moderate disease.
Persistent symptoms, objective weakness/atrophy or failed conservative care warrants injection/surgical referral according to severity.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged systemic analgesic escalation for an entrapment neuropathy that needs mechanical treatment.
Steroid injection requires local procedural/diabetes/anticoagulation risk review.
redFlags: Acute major nerve deficit after trauma
Diffuse neurologic findings suggesting cervical cord or polyneuropathy
counselling: Teach neutral wrist positioning and when weakness rather than numbness should prompt faster reassessment.
followUp: Reassess symptom/function and motor findings; persistent deficit needs definitive evaluation rather than indefinite splint renewal.
examTrap: Ordering MRI for classic nocturnal median-distribution paresthesias before performing a focused neurologic and cervical examination.
oneLinePearl: Carpal tunnel is a localization diagnosis first; tests refine uncertainty and severity.

title: Cervical Radiculopathy: Root Pattern, Conservative Care, and Myelopathy Red Flags
bottomLine: Cervical radiculopathy is a nerve-root syndrome defined by neck/arm pain with dermatomal sensory, myotomal motor or reflex findings. Most uncomplicated cases begin with conservative care; urgent imaging/referral is driven by myelopathy, progressive motor deficit, infection, cancer or major trauma—not pain severity alone.
recognize: Radiating arm pain, paresthesia, focal weakness and reflex asymmetry can localize a cervical root.
Symptoms may worsen with neck position and can coexist with degenerative neck pain.
differentiate: Carpal tunnel/ulnar neuropathy produce peripheral-nerve patterns; shoulder disease causes pain without root neurologic findings.
Myelopathy adds gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, pathologic reflexes or bowel/bladder dysfunction and changes urgency.
assessment: Map dermatomes, strength, reflexes, gait, upper-motor-neuron signs, trauma/cancer/infection risk and functional impact.
workup: Routine immediate imaging is not needed for uncomplicated stable radiculopathy; MRI is appropriate for progressive deficit, myelopathy/red flags or persistent severe symptoms when intervention is being considered.
management: Use activity modification, analgesia and physiotherapy/exercise as appropriate; avoid prolonged immobilization.
Refer urgently for myelopathy/progressive motor loss and routinely for persistent disabling disease or procedural/surgical consideration.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic opioid escalation for uncomplicated radiculopathy.
NSAID and neuropathic-agent choices require renal/GI/falls/sedation risk review.
counselling: Explain that many radiculopathies improve without surgery but progressive weakness or gait/hand dysfunction changes the plan.
followUp: Recheck neurologic deficits and function; document whether weakness is stable, improving or progressing.
examTrap: Ordering urgent MRI solely for severe pain while missing subtle gait hyperreflexia and hand clumsiness that indicate cervical myelopathy.
oneLinePearl: Radiculopathy can wait when stable; myelopathy cannot.
sourceBasis: Canadian spine and neurology practice principles

title: Neuroimaging: Choose CT, MRI, or No Scan From the Clinical Question
bottomLine: Neuroimaging should answer a specific structural or vascular question. Use urgent CT/vascular imaging for selected time-critical hemorrhage/stroke/trauma pathways, MRI for many non-emergent structural/demyelinating/posterior-fossa questions, and no imaging when a validated clinical syndrome has a normal examination and no red flags.
recognize: Imaging yield rises with focal deficit, altered consciousness, thunderclap headache, seizure with concerning context, cancer/immunocompromise, significant trauma or other structural red flags.
Incidental findings are common and can create downstream harm when imaging is used only for reassurance.
differentiate: CT is fast and excellent for acute blood/bone questions but uses ionizing radiation; MRI gives superior soft-tissue detail for many neurologic syndromes but takes longer and has compatibility/logistical limitations.
Typical recurrent migraine, simple syncope with normal neurologic examination and uncomplicated low-back/radicular presentations generally do not need immediate neuroimaging.
assessment: Define onset/timing, focal findings, GCS/mental status, pregnancy, implanted-device/metal history, renal/contrast considerations and exactly what diagnosis the image must confirm/exclude.
workup: Select the modality/protocol matched to the question and use current stroke/trauma/radiology pathways when timing is critical.
Do not substitute a scan for a careful neurologic examination or use repeated imaging without a new management question.
management: Act on urgent imaging findings through the appropriate stroke/neurosurgical/oncology/infectious pathway and ensure incidental/indeterminate findings have proportionate follow-up.
medicationSafety: Contrast decisions require allergy/renal/pregnancy context and the current radiology protocol; avoid treating outdated blanket contraindications as universal.
counselling: Explain when imaging will not improve diagnosis and why avoiding incidental findings/radiation can be safer.
followUp: Track urgent and incidental results to action; do not leave radiology recommendations unowned.
examTrap: Ordering CT/MRI for reassurance in a typical migraine with normal examination while missing a patient whose thunderclap onset actually demands emergency imaging.
oneLinePearl: The right neuroimaging test begins with a specific question; sometimes the right test is no scan.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Neurology, Headache and Radiology recommendations
Canadian Stroke Best Practices where acute stroke imaging applies

title: Neuromuscular Junction Disorders: Localize Fatigable Weakness Before Naming the Disease
bottomLine: Neuromuscular-junction disease causes weakness without a primary sensory level. Use the pattern—fatigability, ocular/bulbar involvement, autonomic symptoms, facilitation and exposure history—to distinguish myasthenia, Lambert-Eaton and botulism, and treat respiratory/bulbar failure as an emergency before confirmatory testing is complete.
recognize: Myasthenia commonly causes fatigable ocular/bulbar/proximal weakness; Lambert-Eaton often has proximal weakness plus autonomic symptoms and reduced reflexes; botulism can produce descending cranial/autonomic paralysis.
differentiate: Peripheral neuropathy usually includes sensory/reflex findings; myopathy is less fluctuating and often has CK/systemic clues; stroke does not produce classic fluctuating fatigability.
assessment: Assess respiratory effort/cough, swallowing/secretions, pupils/autonomic signs, reflexes, sensory examination, medication/toxin/food exposure and cancer risk where Lambert-Eaton is plausible.
workup: Use disease-specific antibodies, electrodiagnostic testing and toxin/public-health testing according to the suspected disorder; do not delay respiratory support for test confirmation.
management: Stabilize airway/ventilation first, then use disorder-specific neurology/toxicology/public-health therapy.
Suspected botulism requires urgent antitoxin/public-health coordination; Lambert-Eaton warrants malignancy evaluation, especially small-cell lung cancer risk.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, magnesium and selected antibiotics can worsen neuromuscular weakness.
Avoid paralytic/sedating medication without anticipating ventilation risk in a patient with marginal neuromuscular respiratory reserve.
redFlags: Weak cough or declining vital capacity
counselling: Teach patients to report swallowing/breathing changes and review new medications with their neuromuscular team.
followUp: Close the loop on malignancy, thymic or toxicologic investigations according to diagnosis.
examTrap: Focusing on antibody testing while a patient with fatigable bulbar weakness is losing respiratory reserve.
oneLinePearl: Localize first, ventilate when needed, then name the neuromuscular-junction disorder.
sourceBasis: Canadian neuromuscular and toxicology practice principles

title: Movement Disorders Beyond Parkinson Disease: Name the Movement Before the Syndrome
bottomLine: Abnormal movement evaluation starts by describing what is actually happening—tremor, chorea, dystonia, tic, myoclonus or medication-induced dyskinesia—before choosing a disease label. Review drugs/toxins and urgent metabolic causes, then refer progressive, disabling or diagnostically uncertain syndromes to movement-disorder expertise.
recognize: Chorea is irregular flowing movement, dystonia causes patterned twisting/posture, myoclonus is shock-like, tics are stereotyped/suppressible with urge in many patients, and tardive dyskinesia follows dopamine-blocking exposure.
differentiate: Akathisia is internal restlessness rather than chorea; tremor differs from myoclonus by rhythmicity; functional movement disorders require positive clinical features rather than diagnosis by exclusion alone.
assessment: Describe movement phenomenology, distribution, triggers, suppressibility, onset/tempo, medication exposure, family history, cognition/psychiatric symptoms and neurologic examination.
workup: Use targeted metabolic, genetic, structural or autoimmune testing based on age/tempo/phenotype; avoid broad panels before accurately classifying the movement.
management: Remove/treat offending medication or reversible cause when safe and use disease-specific symptomatic therapy with neurology guidance.
Tardive syndromes require review of the causative dopamine-blocker and benefit/risk of VMAT2 or other specialty strategies.
medicationSafety: Abruptly stopping antipsychotics can destabilize psychiatric disease; coordinate changes rather than reflex withdrawal.
Dopamine-blocking antiemetics can worsen parkinsonism or cause acute/tardive movement syndromes.
redFlags: Acute movement disorder with fever/rigidity/altered mental status
counselling: Explain the movement phenotype and medication relationship without blaming the patient for involuntary symptoms.
followUp: Track functional disability, medication exposure and progression; refer unexplained/progressive syndromes.
examTrap: Calling every involuntary movement a tremor or Parkinson disease before describing whether it is rhythmic, flowing, twisting or shock-like.
oneLinePearl: Movement-disorder diagnosis begins with phenomenology: name the movement before the disease.

title: Neurologic Manifestations of Systemic Disease: When the Brain Is the Messenger
bottomLine: New neurologic symptoms can be the presenting feature of metabolic, endocrine, hepatic/renal, infectious, autoimmune, malignant or medication disease. Stabilize acute neurologic threats while using systemic clues to avoid anchoring on a primary neurologic diagnosis.
recognize: Hypoglycemia, sodium/calcium disturbance, hepatic/uremic encephalopathy, thyroid/adrenal disease, sepsis, B12 deficiency, vasculitis and cancer can all produce neurologic syndromes.
Medication/toxin effects commonly cause delirium, tremor, neuropathy, seizures or movement disorders.
differentiate: Metabolic encephalopathy tends to be diffuse/fluctuating but can coexist with focal stroke or seizure.
Peripheral neuropathy from diabetes/B12/renal disease differs from acute inflammatory or compressive weakness by tempo and examination pattern.
assessment: Assess ABCs, glucose, mental status, focal deficits, seizure, medication/toxin exposure and systemic symptoms including fever, weight loss, jaundice, renal failure, endocrine or autoimmune clues.
workup: Use targeted metabolic/infectious/autoimmune/oncologic testing guided by syndrome and tempo; image/LP/EEG when a specific neurologic structural/infectious/seizure question remains.
management: Treat immediately reversible systemic threats while managing neurologic complications in parallel.
Escalate focal deficit, meningitis/encephalitis, severe electrolyte disturbance, adrenal crisis, sepsis or rapidly progressive neurologic disease to acute/specialty care.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic failure alters clearance of many neuroactive drugs and can convert a stable dose into toxicity.
Correct sodium/glucose and other metabolic abnormalities at safe syndrome-specific rates rather than chasing normal laboratory values rapidly.
counselling: Explain that neurologic symptoms may improve by treating the systemic disease, but new focal or rapidly progressive findings still require urgent neurologic evaluation.
followUp: Confirm resolution after systemic correction and reassess persistent deficits rather than assuming they were metabolic.
examTrap: Diagnosing primary dementia in a patient with acute confusion from hypoglycemia, sodium disturbance or medication accumulation without first identifying reversible systemic causes.
oneLinePearl: When neurology changes suddenly, check the whole patient—not only the nervous system.
sourceBasis: Canadian neurologic and internal-medicine practice principles
